newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian commerce divided by former front lines.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian commerce divided by former front lines.

text.p: Distrust and nationalist politics limit trade between former enemies in Bosnia who are hesitant to cross sectarian lines despite a peace treaty agreed 18 months ago, a trade official said on Monday.
"Trade between the (Moslem-Croat) federation and the Serb part is legal, but whether it's functioning or not, that's a relative matter," federation deputy trade minister Amir Zukic told Reuters.

"We don't have any official figures of trade volume, but my personal evaluation is that it is not nearly what it could be," Zukic said. "This is more a political problem due to a lack of overall relations rather than some administrative barriers."
The Dayton peace agreement divided Bosnia into two autonomous territories, the Moslem-Croat federation and the Serb republic.
Although the treaty established a small central government to rule over the entities, the agreement has failed to stitch the country back together after a 3-1/2 year war.
Foreign experts confirmed that legal trade between the entities was scarce.
"The inter-entity trade is on a very, very low scale for the same reason the refugees are not going back to their homes," said Mike Sarhan of the U.S. Agency for International Development.
Such a stifling political climate sets the stage for illegal trade, which is thriving in remote areas where black marketeers meet to buy goods safe from the watchful eyes of state inspectors.

Police reports indicate that meat without a veterinarian's seal and cigarettes with false packaging are the most common contraband coming from the Serb entity. The illegal goods are often seized by the truckload.
Conflicting legislation in Bosnia's entities also limits trade, Zukic said.

While the federation treats trade with Bosnian Serbs as internal commerce, Serb regulations require companies trading with federation partners to be registered as foreign export firms and to pay export customs.

"That means the procedure is the same as for foreign trade -- the goods have to be listed and checked by customs officials, sealed and the company needs to pay customs before transporting the goods to federation territory," Zukic said.
Foreign consultants sharply criticised the Serb legislation and have urged an amendment to the package of economic reforms which the central government is currently debating.
"This is absolutely against the Dayton peace agreement and is impeding free trade," Sarhan said. "It should not even be an issue, the trade is inside one country."

Federation and Serb prime ministers signed a landmark agreement last month to re-establish business cooperation between the Ljubia steel ore mine in Serb territory and a steel works factory in the central town of Zenica in the federation.
The trade ministry is now working on final details of the agreement, Zukic said.
"We need to agree on reciprocity of rules, so that both markets are evenly regulated and that we don't have two administrations," he said.
"The basic point is that it should be in the interest of both entities to have as correct a trade as possible, because the state needs to live off something."
